{{short description|Finnish evolutionary biologist}}
'''Virpi Lummaa''' is a Finnish [[Evolutionary biology|evolutionary biologist]] and [[Ecology|ecologist]]. She is an [[Academy of Finland]] professor at the [[University of Turku]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://erc.europa.eu/erc_member/virpi-lummaa|title=Virpi Lummaa|author=<!--Not stated-->|date=n.d.|website=[[European Research Council]]|access-date=2020-06-11}}</ref> Her research interests include [[ageing]], lifespan, and [[natural selection]] in contemporary [[human]] populations.<ref name=":0" /> In addition to her research into [[human evolution]], Lummaa studies life history patterns, social behavior, and more in [[Asian elephant]]s, another large, long-lived [[mammal]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://elephant-project.science/the-team-2/|title=The Team|author=<!--Not stated-->|date=n.d.|website=Myanmar Timber Elephant Project|publisher=[[University of Turku]]|access-date=2020-06-11}}</ref>  Lummaa is currently the Principal Investigator of both the Human Life History Group based at the University of Turku and the [[Myanmar]] Timber Elephant Project.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=https://human-life-history.science/group-members|title=Group Members|author=<!--Not stated-->|date=n.d.|website=Human Life History Group|publisher=University of Turku|access-date=2020-06-11}}</ref> She has received a starting grant from the [[European Research Council]].<ref name=":0" />

== Human life history ==
Lummaa's research into the life history and evolution of contemporary humans has been widely covered by the press. Her work is largely based on a collection of digitized Finnish [[Parish register|parish records]] which provide [[Longitudinal study|longitudinal]] demographic data spanning 350 years and 15 generations.<ref name=":2" /> Lummaa has used these data to investigate a variety of topics related to human survival, reproduction, and evolution in contemporary human populations. She has tested the popular "[[grandmother hypothesis]]" by evaluating the impact of a grandmother's presence on infant survival rates.<ref>{{Cite magazine|last=Yeager|first=Ashley|date=2019-02-07|title='Grandmother Hypothesis' Gets Some Support|url=https://www.the-scientist.com/news-opinion/grandmother-hypothesis-gets-some-support-65441|magazine=[[The Scientist (magazine)|The Scientist]]|access-date=2020-06-11}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2019/02/190207142230.htm|title=Studies Lend Support to 'Grandmother Hypothesis,' but There Are Limits|author=Cell Press|date=2019-02-07|website=[[ScienceDaily]]|access-date=2020-06-11}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|last=Harvey|first=Olivia|date=2019-02-09|title=Kids Benefit from Grandmother Involvement, Until a Certain Point|url=https://www.earth.com/news/kids-benefit-grandmother-healthy/|work=Earth.com|access-date=2020-06-11}}</ref> Overall, her data support the claim that grandmothers can improve infant survival, but noted that there were exceptions. For example, simultaneous child bearing and raising by daughters-in-law and mothers-in-law actually decreased child survival rate.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Devlin|first=Hannah|date=2019-07-26|title=What Is the Menopause and When Does It Strike?|url=https://www.theguardian.com/news/2019/aug/26/what-is-the-menopause-and-when-does-it-strike|work=[[The Guardian]]|access-date=2020-06-11}}</ref> Lummaa has also studied the grandmother hypothesis in Asian elephants. In addition to testing the grandmother hypothesis, Lummaa has used this dataset to evaluate the impact of having a male [[twin]] on females. She found that females with a twin brother had reduced [[fertility]], suggesting a prenatal effect on females with a twin brother.<ref>{{Cite magazine|last=Whyte|first=Chelsea|date=2019-03-18|title=Women with a Twin Brother Are More Likely to Drop Out of School|url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/2196851-women-with-a-twin-brother-are-more-likely-to-drop-out-of-school/|magazine=[[New Scientist]]|access-date=2020-06-11}}</ref> Lummaa has also studied the impact of stressful periods upon miscarriage rates. Interestingly, male fetuses were more likely to be miscarried during difficult times than female fetuses. This resulted in a skewed sex ratio in the population.<ref>{{Cite magazine|last=Pennisi|first=Elizabeth|author-link=Elizabeth Pennisi|date=2014-12-11|title=Why Women's Bodies Abort Males During Tough Times|url=https://www.science.org/content/article/why-women-s-bodies-abort-males-during-tough-times-rev2|magazine=[[Science (journal)|Science]]|access-date=2020-06-11}}</ref>  Furthermore, Lummaa has used this dataset to investigate evolution in contemporary human populations.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Choi|first=Charles Q.|date=2012-04-30|title=Humans Really Are Still Evolving, Study Finds|url=https://www.livescience.com/19993-humans-evolving-natural-selection.html|work=[[Live Science]]|access-date=2020-06-11}}</ref><ref>{{Cite magazine|last=Hullinger|first=Jessica|date=2015-10-26|title=5 Signs Humans Are Still Evolving|url=https://www.mentalfloss.com/article/30795/5-signs-humans-are-still-evolving|magazine=[[Mental Floss]]|access-date=2020-06-11}}</ref>

== Myanmar Timber Elephant Project ==
Through the Myanmar Timber Elephant Project, Lummaa studies similar topics including health, survival and reproduction in Asian elephants. Lummaa argues that despite their appearance, the fact that elephants share long life spans, reproductive history, and family structure with humans makes them useful animals to study.<ref name=":3"/> She hopes that studying elephants can help scientists better understand ageing in humans.<ref name=":3">{{Cite magazine|last=Gillman|first=Steve|date=2019-02-14|title=Elephant Genes Suppress Tumours. Could Studying This Help Us Prevent Cancer?|url=https://horizon-magazine.eu/article/elephant-genes-suppress-tumours-could-studying-help-us-prevent-cancer.html|magazine=[[Horizon (online magazine)|Horizon]]|access-date=2020-06-11}}</ref> This work is based on a century's work of longitudinal demographic data as well as new data collected from live elephants.<ref name=":1" /> These robust datasets exist because captive elephants undergo rigorous health tests throughout their lives to ensure they are fit to work, thereby producing helpful datasets for scientists like Lummaa.<ref name=":3" /> Like her work on humans, Lummaa's research into Asian elephants has been covered in the press. Lummaa has found evidence that elephant grandmothers help care for calves in a role similar to that of human grandmothers.<ref name=":0" /> Additionally, the presence of a maternal sister  improves chance of calf survival.<ref>{{Cite press release|author=<!--Not stated-->|date=2017-07-24|title=Sisters Improve Chances of Reproduction in Asian Elephants|url=https://www.utu.fi/en/news/news/sisters-improve-chances-of-reproduction-in-Asian-elephants|publisher=University of Turku|access-date=2020-06-11}}</ref> Furthermore, her work has revealed that calves born to stressed mothers during harsh weather actually age faster than other calves.<ref name=":3" /> While the exact cause is unclear, Lummaa hopes findings like these can be applied to understand ageing in humans.<ref name=":3" /> In addition to the basic science aim of understanding [[Life history theory|life history]] of large, long-lived mammals such as humans and elephants, the Myanmar Timber Elephant Project hopes their research can guide elephant management and healthcare to improve the lives of captive and wild endangered elephants.<ref name=":1" />  Her research demonstrates that wild populations of Asian elephants are vulnerable to decline.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2019/03/190326202221.htm|title=Future of Elephants Living in Captivity Hangs in the Balance|author=University of Sheffield|date=2019-03-26|website=ScienceDaily|access-date=2020-06-11}}</ref>  She has expressed concern about captive elephant populations used in the timber industry and in tourism. Additionally, she is concerned about the impact these industries have on the wild populations from which the captive population is drawn.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":5">{{Cite news|last=Sharma|first=Ruchira|date=2019-03-28|title=Young Captive Asian Elephants Are Dying Due to the Stress of Being Taken from Their Mothers to Work in Tourism|url=https://inews.co.uk/news/environment/elephants-captive-asia-dying-out-taken-from-mothers-training-273622|work=[[i (newspaper)|i]]|access-date=2020-06-11}}</ref>
